narrative:
The model estimated a 91% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it placed your application in a very high-risk group, and because the law school uses that estimate in admission decisions, your application was rejected. This is a prediction, not a certainty.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That factor had the largest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the second-strongest factor; you were also in the first decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, and it also pushed toward failure. The third most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.10 it was only slightly below the accepted-student average of 3.23, and in this case it worked as a modest counterweight toward passing rather than toward failure.

To move forward, ask admissions for a review meeting and request a clear explanation of what evidence could offset the bar-risk estimate. Ask whether a conditional seat, a bar-readiness plan, or a later reapplication is possible. Strengthen the areas that remain concerning, especially your class-standing record and standardized test preparation, and provide concrete proof of improvement before reapplying.
